euler-identity.name: Euler's identity
euler-identity.oneLiner: The equation that ties the five fundamental constants of mathematics together
euler-identity.description: Euler's identity binds the natural constant e, the imaginary unit i, pi, 1, and 0 into a single compact equation. It follows naturally from Euler's formula once the angle is set to pi, and it stands for the deep connections that run across many branches of mathematics.
euler-identity.significance: It shows that exponentials, trigonometric functions, and complex numbers are all one thing, and it is often called the most beautiful equation in the history of mathematics.

e.description: About 2.71828. It is the base of the natural logarithm and describes continuous growth.

i.description: The number whose square is -1. It is the building block of the complex numbers.

\\pi.description: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. It is about 3.14159.

1.description: The identity for multiplication and the start of the natural numbers.

0.description: The identity for addition, and the value this equation comes out to.

quadratic-formula.name: Quadratic formula
quadratic-formula.oneLiner: The formula that gets the solutions of ax2+bx+c=0 straight from the coefficients
quadratic-formula.description: The quadratic formula computes both roots of a quadratic equation exactly, using nothing but the coefficients a, b, and c. The sign of the discriminant decides how many real roots there are, and this is the most basic solving method in algebra.
quadratic-formula.significance: It is a universal tool that solves every quadratic equation, and through the discriminant it lets you judge whether real roots exist at all.

a.description: The number multiplying x squared. It has to be nonzero for the equation to be quadratic.

b.description: The number multiplying x. It shifts where the axis of the parabola sits.

c.description: The constant added on with no variable attached. It fixes the y-intercept.

b^2-4ac.description: It decides how many roots there are and of what kind. Positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives a repeated root, negative gives imaginary roots.

\\pm.description: It covers the addition and subtraction cases at once, giving both roots.

binomial-theorem.name: Binomial theorem
binomial-theorem.oneLiner: The theorem that expands a power of a sum of two terms using binomial coefficients
binomial-theorem.description: The binomial theorem expands (a+b) to the nth power into a series built from binomial coefficients. It is the key link between combinatorics and algebra, and it is closely tied to Pascal's triangle.
binomial-theorem.significance: It is used widely across mathematics — polynomial expansion, probability, combinatorics — and it provides the basis for approximation.

a.description: The first term of the binomial. Its degree drops as the expansion goes on.

b.description: The second term of the binomial. Its degree rises as the expansion goes on.

n.description: A nonnegative integer saying how many times the binomial is multiplied by itself.

k.description: The summation variable counting how many times b is multiplied in each term.

\\binom{n}{k}.description: The number of ways to choose k things out of n. It matches each entry of Pascal's triangle.

geometric-series.name: Geometric series sum
geometric-series.oneLiner: The formula that gives the sum of a series with a constant ratio in closed form
geometric-series.description: The geometric series formula computes the sum compactly once the first term a and the common ratio r are known. If the absolute value of the ratio is less than 1, even the infinite series converges, and the formula is used all over financial mathematics and physics.
geometric-series.significance: It lets a converging infinite process be written as a finite value, and its practical reach is very wide — compound interest, signal processing, and more.

a.description: The first term of the series. It is the reference value that sets the size of the whole sum.

r.description: The ratio between consecutive terms. Its absolute value must be less than 1 for the infinite series to converge.

n.description: How many terms to add in a finite series.

S_n.description: The sum of the first n terms.

S_{\\infty}.description: The value it converges to, a/(1-r), when the absolute value of the ratio is less than 1.

difference-of-squares.name: Difference of squares
difference-of-squares.oneLiner: The formula that factors a difference of two squares into a product of a sum and a difference
difference-of-squares.description: The difference of squares is the identity saying that a squared minus b squared equals (a+b)(a-b). It is the most basic pattern in factoring, and it also serves for breaking down higher-degree polynomials and for mental arithmetic.
difference-of-squares.significance: It is where algebraic factoring starts, and it turns up everywhere — rationalizing denominators, evaluating limits, factoring integers in number theory.

a.description: The first number or expression being squared.

b.description: The second number or expression being squared.

(a+b).description: The factor made from the sum of a and b.

(a-b).description: The factor made from a minus b.

perfect-square.name: Perfect square expansion
perfect-square.oneLiner: The identity that expands the square of a sum of two terms
perfect-square.description: The perfect square identity says that (a+b) squared equals a squared plus 2ab plus b squared. It is central to factoring quadratics and to recognizing perfect squares, and it underlies solving quadratic equations by completing the square.
perfect-square.significance: It is the most basic tool for reading the structure of a quadratic, and it is essential for converting to vertex form and for minimum-value problems.

a.description: The first term of the binomial being squared.

b.description: The second term of the binomial being squared.

2ab.description: Twice the product of a and b. It is the middle term that shows up in the expansion.

realWorldExamples: Working out how much total area a square garden plot gains when one side is extended by b
Expanding or rearranging the variance formula in statistics

sum-difference-product.name: Product of a sum and a difference
sum-difference-product.oneLiner: The identity that turns a sum times a difference into a difference of squares
sum-difference-product.description: This identity says that (a+b)(a-b) equals a squared minus b squared. It is the same statement as the difference of squares, but read in the multiplying direction rather than the factoring one. It is handy for turning an awkward multiplication into a simple subtraction of squares.
sum-difference-product.significance: It simplifies mental and numerical arithmetic by trading a multiplication for a difference of squares, and it is a key tool for rationalizing and factoring.

a.description: The value that appears in both the sum and the difference.

b.description: The value added to or subtracted from the reference value.

(a+b).description: The factor formed by adding a and b.

(a-b).description: The factor formed by subtracting b from a.

a^2-b^2.description: The result — the difference between the two squares.

realWorldExamples: Clearing an irrational number out of a denominator when rationalizing

arithmetic-series-sum.name: Sum of an arithmetic series
arithmetic-series-sum.oneLiner: The formula for the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence
arithmetic-series-sum.description: The arithmetic series formula multiplies the average of the first and last terms by the number of terms. It is famous from the story of Gauss adding 1 through 100 as a schoolboy, and it is an elegant formula that exploits the symmetry of an arithmetic sequence.
arithmetic-series-sum.significance: It gives a fast total for quantities that rise or fall at a steady rate, and it is fundamental to discrete mathematics and algorithm analysis.

S_n.description: The result of adding up the first n terms.

n.description: The total count of terms being added.

a_1.description: The first term of the sequence.

a_n.description: The nth term of the sequence.

realWorldExamples: Counting the total seats in tiered seating where each row adds a fixed number of seats
Working out a year's total income when a salary rises by a fixed amount every month

arithmetic-general.name: General term of an arithmetic sequence
arithmetic-general.oneLiner: The formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence from its first term and common difference
arithmetic-general.description: This formula adds (n-1) times the common difference to the first term to get any nth term directly. It captures the rule of the sequence in a single expression and makes the linear character of an arithmetic sequence plain.
arithmetic-general.significance: It is the most basic way to pin a sequence's pattern down in a formula, and it provides the bridge to the idea of a function.

a_n.description: The value of the nth term of the sequence.

a_1.description: The starting value of the sequence.

n.description: A natural number saying which term you want.

d.description: The fixed gap between two consecutive terms.

realWorldExamples: Finding the height of floor n when an elevator climbs the same distance every floor
Predicting a value at a given moment when time advances at a steady rate

geometric-series-sum.name: Finite geometric series sum
geometric-series-sum.oneLiner: The formula for the sum of the first n terms of a geometric sequence
geometric-series-sum.description: This formula computes the sum in closed form from the first term, the common ratio, and the number of terms. It applies whenever the ratio is not 1, and the ratio raised to the nth power does the central work. Unlike the general geometric series formula (geometric-series), this one focuses on the finite sum.
geometric-series-sum.significance: It is used directly to quantify exponential change in everyday life — compound interest, installment payments, depreciation.

S_n.description: The sum of the first n terms.

a_1.description: The first term of the series.

r.description: The ratio between consecutive terms. It must not be 1.

n.description: The total count of terms being added.

r^n.description: The ratio multiplied by itself n times. It sets how fast the series grows or converges.

realWorldExamples: Finding the accumulated total after n years of an investment that grows by a fixed percentage annually
Finding the accumulated residue of a drug that breaks down by a fixed fraction each hour

geometric-general.name: General term of a geometric sequence
geometric-general.oneLiner: The formula for the nth term of a geometric sequence from its first term and common ratio
geometric-general.description: This formula multiplies the first term by the common ratio raised to the (n-1)th power to get any nth term directly. It writes the sequence's exponential growth or decay as a single expression.
geometric-general.significance: It is the basic tool for modeling exponential change — population growth, radioactive decay, compound interest.

a_n.description: The value of the nth term of the sequence.

a_1.description: The starting value of the sequence.

r.description: The ratio between two consecutive terms.

n.description: A natural number saying which term you want.

r^{n-1}.description: The ratio multiplied by itself (n-1) times. It is the factor applied to the first term.

realWorldExamples: Counting bacteria after n generations when the colony doubles every generation
Finding the balance after n years on a deposit compounding at a fixed rate

infinite-geometric.name: Infinite geometric series
infinite-geometric.oneLiner: The sum of a geometric series added forever, when the ratio has absolute value less than 1
infinite-geometric.description: This formula shows that when the absolute value of the ratio is under 1, a geometric series settles on a finite value even though it goes on forever. Dividing the first term by (1 minus the ratio) gives that limit. It is the most intuitive example there is for understanding limits and convergence.
infinite-geometric.significance: It is the standard illustration of the mathematical insight that an infinite process can produce a finite result, and it is the starting point of analysis and the theory of series.

S.description: The value that adding infinitely many terms converges to.

a_1.description: The first term of the series.

r.description: The ratio between consecutive terms. Convergence requires |r|<1.

1-r.description: The ratio subtracted from 1. Dividing by it gives the limit.

realWorldExamples: The total distance travelled by a ball that bounces back to a fixed fraction of its height each time it hits the floor
Converting a repeating decimal into a fraction (for instance 0.333... = 1/3)

exponent-law.name: Law of exponents
exponent-law.oneLiner: The law that you add exponents when multiplying powers of the same base
exponent-law.description: This law says that multiplying powers of the same base a is the same as adding the exponents. It follows straight from the definition of a power, and it is the foundation of the whole system of exponent arithmetic. The other laws — for division, for a power of a power — all come out of this one.
exponent-law.significance: It is the most fundamental rule of exponent arithmetic, and it underpins the laws of logarithms, exponential functions, and scientific notation.

a.description: The number the power is built on. It is a nonzero real number.

m.description: The exponent of the first power.

n.description: The exponent of the second power.

m+n.description: The two exponents added together. It is the exponent of the product.

realWorldExamples: Adding exponents to multiply powers of 10 easily in scientific notation
Handling powers of 2 when converting computer memory units

log-definition.name: Definition of the logarithm
log-definition.oneLiner: The equivalence that defines the logarithm as the inverse of exponentiation
log-definition.description: The definition of the logarithm restates, in logarithmic notation, the exponential relation that raising the base a to the power c gives b. It makes the inverse relationship between exponents and logarithms explicit, and it is where logarithmic computation begins.
log-definition.significance: It makes possible the key logarithmic property of turning multiplication into addition, and it is a basic tool of scientific computation and information theory.

a.description: The base of the logarithm. It must be positive and not equal to 1.

b.description: The quantity the logarithm is taken of. It must be positive.

c.description: The number saying what power the base must be raised to in order to give the argument.

\\log_a b.description: The logarithm with base a and argument b.

a^c = b.description: The same relation written as a power.

realWorldExamples: Earthquake magnitude (the Richter scale) is defined on a logarithmic scale, so one step up means about 31.6 times the energy
Loudness (decibels) is measured on a logarithmic scale so that the whole range of human hearing can be handled

log-product-rule.name: Product rule for logarithms
log-product-rule.oneLiner: The law that the logarithm of a product equals the sum of the logarithms
log-product-rule.description: The product rule shows that the logarithm of a product breaks apart into a sum of individual logarithms. It follows directly from the law of exponents and expresses the key logarithmic property of turning multiplication into addition. The quotient rule and the power rule are extensions of the same principle.
log-product-rule.significance: By trading complicated multiplication for simple addition, it revolutionized numerical computation in the age before calculators.

a.description: The first of the positive numbers being multiplied.

b.description: The second of the positive numbers being multiplied.

\\log(ab).description: The logarithm taken of the product of a and b.

realWorldExamples: In astronomy, comparing stellar brightness by turning a brightness ratio into a difference of magnitudes
In information theory, computing the joint information of independent events as a sum of their information contents

complex-plane.name: Complex plane
complex-plane.oneLiner: The plane that pictures a complex number z = a + bi as the point (a, b)
complex-plane.description: The complex plane (the Argand plane) is a two-dimensional coordinate system that puts the real part of a complex number on the horizontal axis and the imaginary part on the vertical one. Every complex number corresponds to a point on the plane, or to a vector from the origin; the modulus |z| is the distance from the origin, and the argument arg(z) is the angle made with the positive real axis. Through polar form and Euler's formula, geometric meanings like rotation and scaling emerge naturally.
complex-plane.significance: It connects the abstract definition of complex numbers to geometric intuition, making complex functions and rotational transformations something you can see.

z.description: A point on the plane made of a real part and an imaginary part.

a.description: The horizontal coordinate of z, Re(z).

b.description: The vertical coordinate of z, Im(z).

|z|.description: The distance from the origin to z. It is sqrt(a^2 + b^2).

\\arg(z).description: The angle between the positive real axis and the vector from the origin to z. It is atan2(b, a).

realWorldExamples: Drawing the impedance of an AC circuit as a vector in the complex plane to see the phase difference
Analyzing the result of a Fourier transform in signal processing as magnitude and phase in the complex plane

linear-transform-2x2.name: 2×2 linear transformation
linear-transform-2x2.oneLiner: The linear map by which a 2×2 matrix M sends a vector in the plane to another vector
linear-transform-2x2.description: A 2×2 linear transformation is the function by which the matrix M = [[a, b], [c, d]] sends every point (x, y) of the plane to (ax + by, cx + dy). The basis vectors e1 and e2 move to the columns of M, the unit square becomes a parallelogram, and the grid becomes a transformed grid. The determinant det(M) gives the change in area together with orientation; when it is 0, a dimension collapses.
linear-transform-2x2.significance: It expresses rotation, reflection, scaling, and shear — every geometric transformation of the plane — as a single matrix, which makes it the basis of computer graphics and linear algebra.

M.description: A 2×2 real matrix. It determines the linear transformation of the plane.

a.description: The horizontal coordinate that the horizontal component of the basis vector e1 takes after the transformation.

b.description: The horizontal coordinate that the horizontal component of the basis vector e2 takes after the transformation.

c.description: The vertical coordinate that the vertical component of the basis vector e1 takes after the transformation.

d.description: The vertical coordinate that the vertical component of the basis vector e2 takes after the transformation.

\\det(M).description: ad - bc. It is the factor by which unit area scales, and its sign gives the orientation.

realWorldExamples: A 2D graphics engine handling rotation, scaling, and shear as a single 2×2 matrix multiplication
Principal component analysis (PCA) extracting the directions of variance in data as eigenvectors of a 2×2 covariance matrix
